title: Multiparameter quantum bounds for entanglement-assisted aperture synthesis
authors: Kalaga Madhav, Pieter Kok, Nic Scott
abstract: Entanglement-assisted optical interferometry promises diffraction-limited imaging over baselines where light cannot be physically combined, but existing theory treats only a single visibility on one two-station baseline. This work formulates the multiparameter estimation problem for an M-station array imaging an extended scene. A reduction lemma shows that the multimode quantum Fisher information (QFI) equals the mean photon number times the QFI of a single delocalized photon, collapsing the problem to a finite-dimensional one. The local photon-number superselection rule (SSR) erases all phase information from the bare state, while shared entanglement restores a fraction f(r)=r/(1+r) of the QFI on a baseline supplied with r pairs -- a factor shown to be achievable, since the reduced two-mode state of any pair is exactly the two-station weak-thermal state. The QFI matrix and its mean Uhlmann curvature reveal numerically that a point source is measurement-compatible, whereas for every extended-source model examined it is incompatible, the Holevo bound exceeding the symmetric-logarithmic-derivative (SLD) bound by up to ~74%. An explicit collective receiver -- a global mode-sorting (quantum Fourier transform) measurement -- then attains a weighted variance within ~7% of the SLD bound and roughly an order of magnitude below an explicit pairwise receiver, and a noisy-resource advantage threshold gives the break-even baseline (~20 km for near-term parameters) beyond which repeater-distributed entanglement beats direct transmission. Finally, the optimal allocation of a finite entanglement budget is a convex program with a closed-form proportional (square-root-law) solution favoring low-visibility baselines. These results recast quantum aperture synthesis as collective multiparameter estimation and give concrete design targets, illustrated on the CHARA array.
summary: This work tackles the quantum limits for imaging with large interferometer arrays by treating the problem as a collective multiparameter estimation task. It shows that optimal measurement requires a global, collective receiver, which significantly beats standard pairwise measurements. The results provide actionable design guidelines, including a threshold determining when distributed entanglement surpasses direct optical links.
main_problem: The paper formulates and solves the multiparameter quantum estimation problem for aperture synthesis using an M-station optical array.
main_result: A collective receiver measurement significantly outperforms pairwise receivers, and the optimal entanglement allocation follows a square-root law favoring low-visibility baselines.
method: The analysis uses the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix, comparing the Holevo bound to the achievable variance using collective measurement strategies.
model_or_system: The system is an M-station optical interferometry setup analyzing the coherence matrix G to estimate the brightness distribution I(s) across multiple baselines.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix, mean Uhlmann curvature, weighted parameter variance, and the incompatibility factor R.
important_parameters: The break-even baseline (L*), the entanglement resource factor f(r) = r/(1+r), and the number of stations M.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the weak thermal light assumption and neglects several effects like transmission loss and finite detector efficiency.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the incompatibility R for point vs. extended sources, compare weighted parameter variance for different receivers (collective vs. pairwise), and show the crossover defining the entanglement advantage threshold L*.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from formulating the multiparameter QFI problem, deriving the reduction lemma, comparing measurement strategies (collective vs. pairwise), determining the resource threshold, and finally solving the optimal entanglement allocation as a convex program.
why_interesting: It provides concrete quantum limits and design targets for quantum sensing in large-scale optical arrays, directly relevant to quantum optics and quantum metrology.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Entanglement-assisted aperture synthesis and the achievable receiver (Sec. 3). (1) Each of M telescopes collects starlight. An entanglement source distributes shared single-photon-entangled ancillas, rij pairs to baseline (i, j). (2) At each station a local receiver—linear optics (a quantum Fourier transform) and photon-number-resolving (PNR) detection—realizes the per-baseline factor f(r) of Eq. (5) using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). (3) A global classical estimator combines the outcomes into visibilities {ˆgij} and the image ˆI(ˆs); approaching the Holevo bound is expected to require this stage to act jointly across baselines (Sec. 5).

Figure 2. Incompatibility R versus separation in units of the resolution element λ/Bmax, for generic M-station arrays and the real CHARA array. R = 0 (desirable) means the SLD bound is attainable and per-baseline processing is optimal; R > 0 means an unavoidable multiparameter penalty [Holevo bound ≤(1 + R)× SLD]. A point source gives R = 0; every extended-source model examined gives R > 0. Numerical details in App. A.

Figure 3. Weighted parameter variance Tr[WJ −1] (per photon) versus source separation for an explicit collective (global QFT) receiver, an explicit pairwise (beam-splitter) receiver, and the SLD (QFI) bound, for a two-point source on a generic M = 6 array. The collective receiver tracks the SLD bound to within ∼7%; the pairwise receiver is ∼10× worse. App. A.

Figure 4. Noisy-resource advantage threshold. (a) Per-baseline phase QFI versus baseline length L: direct interferometry decays with fibre loss, while entanglement assistance is set by the (length-independent) repeater efficiency; they cross at L⋆≈20 km. (b) Break-even baseline L⋆of Eq. (11) over the Bell-fidelity/repeater-efficiency plane.

Figure 5. Entanglement allocation on the CHARA array (15 baselines, two-point source at 1 mas). (a) Proportional rule (12) per baseline, sorted by visibility (lowest γij on top, annotated). (b) Proportional versus true water-filling allocation. Numerical details in App. A.
